opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important question, and my view is that we shouldn't treat it as an either-or. There's this framing sometimes of "Transformers versus the alternatives," but a huge amount of what the community has learned over the last several years with Transformers is directly transferable, and we'd be foolish to throw it away.

At one level, a lot of the progress in deep learning isn't really about the sequence mixing layer at all. It's about everything around it: normalization choices, the MLP blocks, residual structure, how you set up training, optimizer details, data pipelines, scaling recipes, tokenization. When we were developing Mamba, for example, a big part of making it work well in practice was just adopting the modern Transformer recipe and swapping out the attention component. So the backbone design wisdom carries over almost entirely.

At a deeper level, I think Transformers have taught us something about what properties matter. Attention is extremely good at certain things, like precise retrieval and recall from context, because it keeps the whole history around in a cache. Recurrent or state space models compress the history into a fixed-size state, which makes them efficient but means they have to be selective about what they remember. Understanding those tradeoffs clearly, rather than declaring one approach better, is what should guide design. That's partly why I think hybrid models, which interleave some attention layers with state space layers, have turned out to be so effective. They let each component do what it's good at.

There's also the systems side. A lot of Transformer progress came from being hardware-aware, things like FlashAttention showing that how you map computation onto GPUs matters as much as the asymptotic complexity. Post-Transformer architectures have to take that lesson seriously. An idea that looks great on paper but doesn't run efficiently on real accelerators isn't going to get adopted.

And finally, I'd say the mechanistic understanding people have built up, things like induction heads, in-context learning behavior, associative recall tasks, gives us really useful diagnostic tools. We can use those synthetic tasks to probe new architectures and understand where they fall short before spending tons of compute scaling them up.

So my general philosophy is: learn from Transformers deeply, keep what works, and be very precise about which specific limitations you're trying to address, whether that's efficiency on long sequences, inference cost, or something about the inductive bias. That's how you make real progress rather than just proposing something different for the sake of being different.

r001.rationale: The response discusses carrying Transformer design lessons into Mamba and hybrid models, but it does not propose distilling a pretrained Transformer into a state model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really important question, and I'd say my perspective on it has shifted a bit over the years. When we started working on state space models, there was a bit of a temptation to think of it as, you know, "we're going to do something completely different from Transformers." And I think that framing is actually wrong, or at least not very productive.

The way I think about it now is that the Transformer isn't really one thing. It's a bundle of design decisions that happened to get made together, and some of them are about the attention mechanism specifically, and a lot of them aren't. There's the residual stream, the pre-norm, the MLP blocks, the whole macro architecture of stacking these blocks. There's the training recipe, the optimizer choices, the learning rate schedules, the scaling laws people have worked out. And then there's a huge amount of systems work, like how you actually get these things to run efficiently on hardware, mixed precision, all of that.

And almost none of that is actually about attention. So when we were developing Mamba, a lot of what we did was basically just keep everything that works and swap out the one piece we actually had a different opinion about. The Mamba block looks a lot like a Transformer block for that reason. We're not trying to reinvent normalization. We're trying to replace the sequence mixing layer.

I think the other thing the Transformer era taught us, which is maybe less obvious, is what matters empirically versus what people thought mattered. There were years of papers on efficient attention variants, linear attention, sparse attention, all these things, and a lot of them worked okay on benchmarks but didn't really hold up at scale or on the tasks people actually cared about. And that history is really informative, because it tells you where the failure modes are. Things like in-context retrieval, copying, associative recall, these turned out to be the things that distinguish a model that works from one that looks good on paper. So we actually use those as sort of litmus tests now. If you're proposing a new architecture, you'd better be able to explain how it handles those, because the attention literature already showed us that's where things break.

And then the last piece is, honestly, attention is really good. There's a reason it won. So I don't think "post-Transformer" should mean "no attention." I think the more likely outcome is hybrids, where you have mostly efficient recurrent or state space layers and a small number of attention layers that give you that precise retrieval capability. And a lot of the recent work, from us and from others, has been pointing in that direction. So the Transformer work doesn't just inform the next generation, it's probably literally a component of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retaining Transformer design choices, replacing the sequence mixing layer, and using hybrid architectures, but it does not propose distilling a pretrained Transformer into a state model.

astra-6.text:
I think we should learn as much as we can from it. There’s an enormous amount of work that’s gone into making Transformers effective, and a lot of that isn’t necessarily specific to attention. Things like the training recipe, the data, the way you organize the blocks—those are potentially useful for other architectures too.

That also makes comparisons tricky. If you take a new architecture and compare it against a Transformer that’s had years of tuning, you’re comparing more than just the underlying architectural ideas. But you also can’t assume that every choice that works well for a Transformer is the right choice for the new model.

So I think the approach is to borrow what you can, while being deliberate about testing those assumptions. And studying where Transformers work well is useful in itself. What does attention give you that another mechanism struggles to reproduce? Where is it expensive, and can you get the behavior you need more efficiently? The goal is to understand those tradeoffs and build better models, which may include combining ideas from different architectures.

r001.rationale: The response discusses borrowing and testing Transformer design choices, but it does not propose distilling a pretrained Transformer into a state model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot to learn from Transformers, and we should be careful about what we’re actually trying to replace. A Transformer is a whole architecture, and attention is one component of it. Things like the residual connections, the normalization, the feedforward layers, and the training recipe all carry a lot of accumulated knowledge. If you change all of those at once, it becomes hard to understand where an improvement is coming from.

So one productive approach is to keep much of that framework and ask: can we replace the sequence-mixing component with something that has different tradeoffs? Can we get more efficient inference or handle longer sequences while preserving the capabilities people care about?

And the successes of attention should inform that design. Its ability to selectively access information based on the input is very useful. An alternative doesn’t necessarily need to implement that in the same way, but it needs to address why that capability matters. I think the goal is to understand which principles make Transformers work and find other ways to realize them, rather than treating everything associated with Transformers as something we need to discard.

r001.rationale: The response discusses replacing the sequence-mixing component and learning from Transformer principles, but does not propose distilling a pretrained Transformer into a state model.
